entries.bc615041773fcd025ba69ce8ff0ca8acfcdaeafa: <div eID="gen23810" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23811" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23812" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23812" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23811" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23813" type="x-p"/> The preceptor calls his pupils, and tells them how himself was educated, <reference osisRef="Pro.4.1-Pro.4.4">Pro 4:1-4</reference>; specifies the teachings he received, <reference osisRef="Pro.4.5-Pro.4.19">Pro 4:5-19</reference>; and exhorts his pupil to persevere in well-doing, and to avoid evil, <reference osisRef="Pro.4.20-Pro.4.27">Pro 4:20-27</reference>. <div eID="gen23813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23814" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23815" type="x-p"/> Hear, ye children - Come, my pupils, and hear how a father instructed his child. Such as I received from my father I give to you, and they were the teachings of a wise and affectionate parent to his only son, a peculiar object of his regards, and also those of a fond mother. <div eID="gen23815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23816" type="x-p"/> He introduces the subject thus, to show that the teaching he received, and which he was about to give them, was the most excellent of its kind. By this he ensured their attention, and made his way to their heart. Teaching by precept is good; teaching by example is better; but teaching both by precept and example is best of all.
entries.b0f7ef8a0e294b624a3e0cee05a291b8ba413194: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23817" type="x-p"/> He taught me also, and said - Open thy heart to receive my instructions - receive them with affection; when heard, retain and practice them; and thou shalt live - the great purpose of thy being brought into the world shall be accomplished in thee.
entries.a2f762c4a17ec87a698af4fd11255343612006a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23818" type="x-p"/> Get wisdom - True religion is essential to thy happiness; never forget its teachings, nor go aside from the path it prescribes.
entries.3c762966b1df19e0a71888e36240d81ab4615fb4: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23819" type="x-p"/> Forsake her not - Wisdom personified is here represented as a guardian and companion, who, if not forsaken, will continue faithful; if loved, will continue a protector.
entries.8c71399b94e91e9e5a5b6dca09631b3bced3b8a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23820" type="x-p"/> Wisdom is the principal thing - ראשית חכמה reshith chochmah, "wisdom is the principle." It is the punctum saliens in all religion to know the true God, and what he requires of man, and for what he has made man; and to this must be added, under the Christian dispensation, to know Jesus Christ whom he hath sent, and for what end He was sent, the necessity of his being sent, and the nature of that salvation which he has bought by his own blood. <div eID="gen23820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23821" type="x-p"/> Get wisdom - Consider this as thy chief gain; that in reference to which all thy wisdom, knowledge, and endeavors should be directed. <div eID="gen23821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23822" type="x-p"/> And with all thy getting - Let this be thy chief property. While thou art passing through things temporal, do not lose those things which are eternal; and, while diligent in business, be fervent in spirit, serving the Lord. <div eID="gen23822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23823" type="x-p"/> Get understanding - Do not be contented with the lessons of wisdom merely; do not be satisfied with having a sound religious creed; devils believe and tremble; but see that thou properly comprehend all that thou hast learnt; and see that thou rightly apply all that thou hast been taught. <div eID="gen23823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23824" type="x-p"/> Wisdom prescribes the best end, and the means best calculated for its attainment. Understanding directs to the ways, times, places, and opportunities of practicing the lessons of wisdom. Wisdom points out the thing requisite; understanding sees to the accomplishment and attainment. Wisdom sees; but understanding feels. One discovers, the other possesses. <div eID="gen23824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23825" type="x-p"/> Coverdale translates this whole verse in a very remarkable manner: "The chefe poynte of wyssdome is, that thou be wyllynge to opteyne wyssdome; and before all thy goodes to get the understandynge." This is paraphrase, not translation. In this version paraphrase abounds. <div eID="gen23825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23826" type="x-p"/> The translation in my old MS. Bible is very simple: Begynnynge of wisdam, welle thou wisdom; in al thi wisdam, and in al thi possioun, purchas prudence. He is already wise who seeks wisdom; and he is wise who knows its value, seeks to possess it. The whole of this verse is wanting in the Arabic, and in the best copies of the Septuagint. <div eID="gen23826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23827" type="x-p"/> Instead of קנה חכמה keneh chochmah, get wisdom, the Complutensian Polyglot has קנה בינה keneh binah, get understanding; so that in it the verse stands, "Wisdom is the principle, get understanding; and in all this getting, get understanding." This is not an error either of the scribe, or of the press, for it is supported by seven of the MSS. of Kennicott and De Rossi. <div eID="gen23827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23828" type="x-p"/> The Complutensian, Antwerp, and Paris Polyglots have the seventh verse in the Greek text; but the two latter, in general, copy the former.
entries.a4ef77f61f8b934479f0286ea0cbb4855ee40a76: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23829" type="x-p"/> She shall bring thee to honor - There is nothing, a strict life of piety and benevolence excepted, that has such a direct tendency to reflect honor upon a man, as the careful cultivation of his mind. One of Bacon's aphorisms was, Knowledge is power; and it is truly astonishing to see what influence true learning has. Nothing is so universally respected, provided the learned man be a consistent moral character, and be not proud and overbearing; which is a disgrace to genuine literature.
entries.a01c3486136fa04b59d7b5bef603f1fae8649f47: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen23829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23830" type="x-p"/> A crown of glory - A tiara, diadem, or crown, shall not be more honorable to the princely wearer, than sound wisdom - true religion - coupled with deep learning, shall be to the Christian and the scholar.
entries.7f1471c717cbc28f068cbff44f9beda1eddee1a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen23830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23831" type="x-p"/> The years of thy life shall be many - Vice and intemperance impair the health and shorten the days of the wicked; while true religion, sobriety, and temperance, prolong them. The principal part of our diseases springs from "indolence, intemperance, and disorderly passions." Religion excites to industry, promotes sober habits, and destroys evil passions, and harmonizes the soul; and thus, by preventing many diseases, necessarily prolongs life.
entries.6f3c58a6792c2e058edfd6814f38c6b55e43eae9: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen23831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23832" type="x-p"/> Thy steps shall not be straitened - True wisdom will teach thee to keep out of embarrassments. A man under the influence of true religion ponders his paths, and carefully poises occurring circumstances; and as the fear of God will ever lead him to act an upright and honest part, so his way in business and life is both clear and large. He has no by-ends to serve; he speculates not; he uses neither trick nor cunning to effect any purpose. Such a man can never be embarrassed. His steps are not straitened; he sees his way always plain; and when a favorable tide of Providence shows him the necessity of increased exertion, he runs, and is in no danger of stumbling.
entries.45abd23fdc536994c2be51e67c6e99c7d47e649e: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen23832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23833" type="x-p"/> Take fast hold - החזק hachazek, seize it strongly, and keep the hold; and do this as for life. Learn all thou canst, retain what thou hast learnt, and keep the reason continually in view - it is for thy life.
entries.5b2636f7c943bbe4081ff680def2ad3f6886c1d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen23833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23834" type="x-p"/> Enter not into the path of the wicked - Never associate with those whose life is irregular and sinful; never accompany them in any of their acts of transgression.
entries.4a14e0d43f1ae0a6c61272130cbd275b870ee96e: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen23834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23835" type="x-p"/> Avoid it - Let it be the serious purpose of thy soul to shun every appearance of evil. <div eID="gen23835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23836" type="x-p"/> Pass not by it - Never, for the sake of worldly gain, or through complaisance to others, approach the way that thou wouldst not wish to be found in when God calls thee into the eternal world. <div eID="gen23836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23837" type="x-p"/> Turn from it - If, through unwatchfulness or unfaithfulness, thou at any time get near or into the way of sin, turn from it with the utmost speed, and humble thyself before thy Maker. <div eID="gen23837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23838" type="x-p"/> And pass away - Speed from it, run for thy life, and get to the utmost distance; eternally diverging so as never to come near it whilst thou hast a being.
entries.70966628b038b4ae15f680185eb42ca7f1bee965: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen23838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23839" type="x-p"/> Except they have done mischief - The night is their time for spoil and depredation. And they must gain some booty, before they go to rest. This I believe to be the meaning of the passage. I grant, also, that there may be some of so malevolent a disposition that they cannot be easy unless they can injure others, and are put to excessive pain when they perceive any man in prosperity, or receiving a kindness. The address in Virgil, to an illnatured shepherd is well known: - <div eID="gen23839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23840" type="x-p"/> Et cum vidisti puero donata, dolebas: <div eID="gen23840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23841" type="x-p"/> Et si non aliqua nocuisses, mortuus esses. <div eID="gen23841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23842" type="x-p"/> Eclog. 3: 14. "When thou sawest the gifts given to the lad, thou wast distressed; and hadst thou not found some means of doing him a mischief, thou hadst died."
entries.e98e0327aeea35c12124327d4d6a7446c40ada1a: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen23842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23843" type="x-p"/> For they eat the bread of wickedness - By privately stealing. <div eID="gen23843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23844" type="x-p"/> And drink the wine of violence - By highway robbery.
entries.243f5d1990ee1a08ca4ae327cdad1b891d1f309d: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen23844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23845" type="x-p"/> But the path of the just - The path of the wicked is gloomy, dark, and dangerous; that of the righteous is open, luminous, and instructive. This verse contains a fine metaphor; it refers to the sun rising above the horizon, and the increasing twilight, till his beams shine full upon the earth. The original, הולך ואור עד נכון היום holech vaor ad nechon haiyom, may be translated, "going and illuminating unto the prepared day." This seems plainly to refer to the progress of the rising sun while below the horizon; and the gradual increase of the light occasioned by the reflection of his rays by means of the atmosphere, till at last he is completely elevated above the horizon, and then the prepared day has fully taken place, the sun having risen at the determined time. So, the truly wise man is but in his twilight here below; but he is in a state of glorious preparation for the realms of everlasting light; till at last, emerging from darkness and the shadows of death, he is ushered into the full blaze of endless felicity. Yet previously to his enjoyment of this glory, which is prepared for him, he is going - walking in the commandments of his God blameless; and illuminating - reflecting the light of the salvation which he has received on all those who form the circle of his acquaintance.
entries.be7d74dbf7a10de322fec880e323e2d5af1d2452: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen23845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23846" type="x-p"/> Keep them in the midst of thine heart - Let them be wrapped up in the very center of thy affections; that they may give spring and energy to every desire, word, and wish.
entries.b3482798d057e6681de8998c7e35298b38e6c75f: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen23846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23847" type="x-p"/> Keep thy heart with all diligence - "Above all keeping," guard thy heart. He who knows any thing of himself, knows how apt his affections are to go astray. <div eID="gen23847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23848" type="x-p"/> For out of it are the issues of life - תוצאות חיים totseoth chaiyim, "the goings out of lives." Is not this a plain allusion to the arteries which carry the blood from the heart through the whole body, and to the utmost extremities? As long as the heart is capable of receiving and propelling the blood, so long life is continued. Now as the heart is the fountain whence all the streams of life proceed, care must be taken that the fountain be not stopped up nor injured. A double watch for its safety must be kept up. So in spiritual things: the heart is the seat of the Lord of life and glory; and the streams of spiritual life proceed from him to all the powers and faculties of the soul. Watch with all diligence, that this fountain be not sealed up, nor these streams of life be cut off. Therefore "put away from thee a froward mouth and perverse lips - and let thy eyes look straight on." Or, in other words, look inwardlook onward - look upward. <div eID="gen23848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23849" type="x-p"/> I know that the twenty-third verse is understood as principally referring to the evils which proceed from the heart, and which must be guarded against; and the good purposes that must be formed in it, from which life takes its colouring. The former should be opposed; the latter should be encouraged and strengthened. If the heart be pure and holy, all its purposes will be just and good. If it be impure and defiled, nothing will proceed from it but abomination. But though all this be true, I have preferred following what I believe to be the metaphor in the text.
entries.fd10ecb21676f564cffa13b50424141aebb5c362: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen23849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23850" type="x-p"/> A froward mouth - Beware of hastiness, anger, and rash speeches. <div eID="gen23850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23851" type="x-p"/> And perverse lips - Do not delight in nor acquire the habit of contradicting and gainsaying; and beware of calumniating and backbiting your neighbor.
entries.df4fee9c8242364a89f7380c7a328f37dac7b41c: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen23851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23852" type="x-p"/> Ponder the path of thy feet - Weigh well the part thou shouldst act in life. See that thou contract no bad habits.
entries.2dbeda0c900c3d5772cc215878dc3e7aa554450d: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen23852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23853" type="x-p"/> Turn not to the right hand nor to the left - Avoid all crooked ways. Be an upright, downright, and straight-forward man. Avoid tricks, wiles, and deceptions of this kind. <div eID="gen23853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23854" type="x-p"/> To this the Septuagint and Vulgate add the following verse: Αυτος δε ορθας ποιησει τας τροχιας σου, τας δε πορειας σου εν ειρηνη προαξει. Ipse autem rectos faciet cursus tuos; itinera autem tua in pace producet. "For himself will make thy paths straight and thy journeyings will he conduct in prosperity." The Arabic has also a clause to the same effect. But nothing like this is found in the Hebrew, Chaldee, or Syriac; nor in the Vulgate, as printed in the Complutensian Polyglot; nor in that of Antwerp or of Paris; but it is in the Greek text of those editions, in the editio princeps of the Vulgate, in five of my own MSS., and in the old MS. Bible. De Lyra rejects the clause as a gloss that stands on no authority. If an addition, it is certainly very ancient; and the promise it contains is true whether the clause be authentic or not.  <chapter eID="Prov.4"/> <div eID="gen23854" type="x-p"/>

entries.b7ff61d2424081d8e8da11e25bd0fb683cce42bb: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.1-Prov.4.4">Pro 4:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen10663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10664" type="x-p"/> He now confirms and explains the command to duty which he has placed at the beginning of the whole (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.8">Pro 1:8</reference>). This he does by his own example, for he relates from the history of his own youth, to the circle of disciples by whom he sees himself surrounded, what good doctrine his parents had taught him regarding the way of life: 1 Hear, ye sons, the instruction of a father,    And attend that ye may gain understanding; 2 For I give to you good doctrine,    Forsake not my direction! 3 For I was a son to my father,    A tender and only (son) in the sight of my mother. 4 And he instructed me, and said to me:    “Let thine heart hold fast my words:    Observe my commandments and live!” <div eID="gen10664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10665" type="x-p"/> That בּנים in the address comes here into the place of בּני, hitherto used, externally denotes that בני in the progress of these discourses finds another application: the poet himself is so addressed by his father. Intentionally he does not say אביכם (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.1.8">Pro 1:8</reference>): he does not mean the father of each individual among those addressed, but himself, who is a father in his relation to them as his disciples; and as he manifests towards them fatherly love, so also he can lay claim to paternal authority over them. לדעת is rightly vocalized, not לדעת. The words do not give the object of attention, but the design, the aim. The combination of ideas in דּעת בּינה (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.1.2">Pro 1:2</reference>), which appears to us singular, loses its strangeness when we remember that דעת means, according to its etymon, deposition or reception into the conscience and life. Regarding לקח, apprehension, reception, lesson = doctrine, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Pro 1:5. נתתּי is the perf., which denotes as fixed and finished what is just now being done, Gesenius, §126, 4. עזב is here synonym of נטשׁ, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.8">Pro 1:8</reference>, and the contrary of שׁמר, Pro 28:4. The relative <hi type="italic">factum</hi> in the perfect, designating the circumstances under which the event happened, regularly precedes the chief <hi type="italic">factum</hi> ויּרני; see under Gen 1:2. Superficially understood, the expression 3a would be a platitude; the author means that the natural legal relation was also confirming itself as a moral one. It was a relation of many-sided love, according to 3a: he was esteemed of his mother - לפני, used of the reflex in the judgment, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.9">Gen 10:9</reference>, and of loving care, <reference osisRef="Gen.17.18">Gen 17:18</reference>, means this - as a tender child, and therefore tenderly to be protected (רך as <reference osisRef="Gen.33.13">Gen 33:13</reference>), and as an only child, whether he were so in reality, or was only loved as if he were so. יחיד (Aq., Sym., Theod., μονογενής) may with reference to number also mean <hi type="italic">unice dilectus</hi> (lxx ἀγαπώμενος); cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.22.2">Gen 22:2</reference>, יחידך (where the lxx translate τὸν ἀγαπητόν, without therefore having ידידך before them). לפני is maintained by all the versions; לבני is not a variant.<note placement="foot">In some editions לבני is noted as Kerı̂ to לפני, but erroneously and contrary to the express evidence of the Masora, which affirms that there are two passages in which we ought to read not לפני, but לבני, viz., <reference osisRef="Ps.80.3">Psa 80:3</reference> and Pro 4:3.</note> <div eID="gen10665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10666" type="x-p"/> The instruction of the father begins with the jussive, which is pointed יתמך־<note placement="foot">The writing of -יתמך with the grave <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> (<hi type="italic">Gaja</hi>) and <hi type="italic">Kametz-Chatuph</hi> (ǒ) is that of Ben Asher; on the other hand, יתמך־ with Cholem (ō) and the permanent <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> is that of Ben Naphtali; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 21a [under the verbal form 25], §30.</note> to distinguish it from יתמך־ on account of the ǒ. The lxx has incorrectly ἐρειδέτω, as if the word were יסמך; Symmachus has correctly κατεχέτω. The imper. וחיה is, as <reference osisRef="Prov.7.2">Pro 7:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.20.7">Gen 20:7</reference>, more than ותחיה; the teacher seeks, along with the means, at the same time their object: Observe my commandments, and so become a partaker of life! The Syriac, however, adds תּורתיו כּאישׁון עיניך and my instruction as the apple of thine eye, a clause borrowed from Pro 7:2.
entries.36373f6705ffc969c6b53a10df7be7910917e09e: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.5-Prov.4.6">Pro 4:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen10666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10667" type="x-p"/> The exhortation of the father now specializes itself: 5 Get wisdom, get understanding;    Forget not and turn not from the words of my mouth. 6 Forsake her not, so shall she preserve thee;    Love her, so shall she keep thee. <div eID="gen10667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10668" type="x-p"/> Wisdom and understanding are (5a) thought of as objects of merchandise (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.23.23">Pro 23:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.14">Pro 3:14</reference>), like the one pearl of great price, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.46">Mat 13:46</reference>, and the words of fatherly instruction (5b), accordingly, as offering this precious possession, or helping to the acquisition of it. One cannot indeed say correctly אל־תשׁכח מאמרי־פי, but אל־תשׁכח משּׁמר אמרי־פי (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.5">Psa 102:5</reference>); and in this sense אל־תּשׁכּח goes before, or also the accus. object, which in אל־תשכח the author has in his mind, may, since he continues with אל־תּט, now not any longer find expression as such. That the אמרי־פי are the means of acquiring wisdom is shown in <reference osisRef="Prov.4.6">Pro 4:6</reference>, where this continues to be the primary idea. The verse, consisting of only four words, ought to be divided by <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>;<note placement="foot">According to correct readings in codd. and older editions, ותשמרךּ has also indeed <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi> <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>, and אהבה, <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> (with <hi type="italic">Zinnorith</hi>); <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 47, §6; <hi type="italic">Accentuationssystem</hi>, xviii. §1, 2; and regarding the <hi type="italic">Zinnorith</hi>, see <hi type="italic">Liber Psalmorum Hebraicus</hi> by S. Baer, p. xii.</note> the <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> (ו) in both halves of the verse introduces the <hi type="italic">apodosis imperativi</hi> (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Pro 3:9., and the <hi type="italic">apodosis prohibitivi</hi>, Pro 3:21.). The actual representation of wisdom, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.5">Pro 4:5</reference>, becomes in <reference osisRef="Prov.4.6">Pro 4:6</reference> personal.
entries.089a2d308eeff62ad4550f8bdc74be2842efc4ce: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.7-Prov.4.9">Pro 4:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen10668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10669" type="x-p"/> Referring to <reference osisRef="Prov.4.5">Pro 4:5</reference>, the father further explains that wisdom begins with the striving after it, and that this striving is itself its fundamental beginning: 7 The beginning of wisdom is “Get wisdom,”    And with [um, at the price of] all thou hast gotten get understanding, 8 Esteem her, so shall she lift thee up;    She will bring thee honour if thou dost embrace her. 9 She will put on thine head a graceful garland,    She will bestow upon thee a glorious diadem. <div eID="gen10669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10670" type="x-p"/> In the motto of the book, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.7">Pro 1:7</reference>, the author would say that the fear of Jahve is that from which all wisdom takes its origin. יראת יהוה (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.7">Pro 1:7</reference>) is the subject, and as such it stands foremost. Here he means to say what the beginning of wisdom consists in. ראשׁית חכמה is the subject, and stands forth as such. The predicate may also be read קנה־חכמה (= קנות), after Pro 16:16. The beginning of wisdom is (consists in) the getting of wisdom; but the imperative קנה, which also Aq., Sym., Theod. (κτῆσαι), Jerome, Syr., Targ. express (the lxx leaves <reference osisRef="Prov.4.7">Pro 4:7</reference> untranslated), is supported by 7b. Hitzig, after Mercier, De Dieu, and Döderlein, translates the verse thus: “the highest thing is wisdom; get wisdom,” which Zöckler approves of; but the reasons which determine him to this rendering are subtleties: if the author had wished himself to be so understood, he ought at least to have written the words ראשׁית החכמה. But ראשׁית חכמה is a genitive of relation, as is to be expected from the relativity of the idea ראשׁית, and his intention is to say that the beginning of wisdom consists in the proposition קנה חכמה (cf. the similar formula, <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.13">Ecc 12:13</reference>); this proposition is truly the <hi type="italic">lapis philosophorum</hi>, it contains all that is necessary in order to becoming wise. Therefore the Greek σοφία called itself modestly φιλοσοφία; for ἀρχὴ σὐτῆς the Book of Wisdom has, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.18">Pro 6:18</reference>, ἡ ἀληθεστάτη παιδείας ἐπιθυμία. In 7b the proposition is expressed which contains the <hi type="italic">specificum</hi> helping to wisdom. The בּ denotes price: give all for wisdom (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.46">Mat 13:46</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.44">Mat 13:44</reference>); no price is too high, no sacrifice too great for it.
entries.213b8c71788edf1906d28c0b5e6b46de7876201f: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.10-Prov.4.12">Pro 4:10-12</reference> <div eID="gen10671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10672" type="x-p"/> There is no reason for the supposition that the warning which his father gave to the poet now passes over into warnings given by the poet himself (Hitzig); the admonition of the father thus far refers only in general to the endeavour after wisdom, and we are led to expect that the good doctrines which the father communicates to the son as a <hi type="italic">viaticum</hi> will be further expanded, and become more and more specific when they take a new departure. 10 Hearken, my son, and receive my sayings,      So shall the years of life be increased to thee. 11 In the way of wisdom have I taught thee,      Guided thee in the paths of rectitude. 12 When thou goest, thy step shall not be straitened;      And if thou runnest, thou shalt not stumble. <div eID="gen10672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10673" type="x-p"/> Regarding קח (of לקח) of appropriating reception and taking up in <hi type="italic">succum et sanguinem</hi>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.1.3">Pro 1:3</reference>; regarding שׁנות חיּים, years not merely of the duration of life, but of the enjoyment of life, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.2">Pro 3:2</reference>; regarding מעגּל (מעגּלה), path (track), <reference osisRef="Prov.2.9">Pro 2:9</reference>; regarding the בּ of הורה, of the department and subject of instruction, Psa 25:8. The perfects, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.11">Pro 4:11</reference>, are different from נתתּי, 2a: they refer to rules of life given at an earlier period, which are summarily repeated in this address. The way of wisdom is that which leads to wisdom (<reference osisRef="Job.28.23">Job 28:23</reference>); the paths of rectitude, such as trace out the way which is in accordance with the rule of the good and the right. If the youth holds to this direction, he will not go on in darkness or uncertainty with anxious footsteps; and if in youthful fervour he flies along his course, he will not stumble on any unforeseen obstacle and fall. יצר is as a metaplastic fut. to צרר or צוּר, to be narrow, to straiten, formed as if from יצר. The Targ. after Aruch,<note placement="foot">R. Nathan ben Jechiel, a.d. 1106, who is usually styled by the Jewish writers בּעל ערוּך, Auctor Aruch, author of a Talmudical Lexicon.</note> לא תשנק ארחך, thou shalt not need to bind together (<hi type="italic">constringere</hi>) or to hedge up thy way.
entries.4201a7efa17e9803ee77e306cb3bb382ba3bb455: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.13-Prov.4.14">Pro 4:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen10673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10674" type="x-p"/> The exhortations attracting by means of promises, now become warnings fitted to alarm: 13 Hold fast to instruction, let her not go;      Keep her, for she is thy life. 14 Into the path of the wicked enter not,      And walk not in the way of the evil 15 Avoid it, enter not into it;      Turn from it and pass away. 16 For they cannot sleep unless they do evil,      And they are deprived of sleep unless they bring others to ruin. 17 For they eat the bread of wickedness,      And they drink the wine of violence. <div eID="gen10674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10675" type="x-p"/> Elsewhere מוּסר means also self-discipline, or moral religious education, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.3">Pro 1:3</reference>; here discipline, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, parental educative counsel. תּרף is the segolated fut. apoc. <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. (indic. תּרפּה) from tarp, cf. the imper. <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הרף from harp. נצּרה is the imper. <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> (not <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, as Aben Ezra thinks) with <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> <hi type="italic">dirimens</hi>; cf. the verbal substantive נצּרה <reference osisRef="Ps.141.3">Psa 141:3</reference>, with similar <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi>, after the form יקּהה, Gen 49:10. מוּסר (elsewhere always masc.) is here used in the fem. as the synonym of the name of wisdom: keep her (instruction), for she is thy life,<note placement="foot">Punctuate כּי היא; the <hi type="italic">Zinnorith</hi> represents the place of the <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 9.</note><hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the life of thy life. In <reference osisRef="Prov.4.14">Pro 4:14</reference> the godless (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., on the root-idea of רשׁע under <reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Psa 1:1</reference>) and the habitually wicked, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the vicious, stand in parallelism; בּוא and אשּׁר are related as entering and going on, <hi type="italic">ingressus</hi> and <hi type="italic">progressus</hi>. The verb אשׁר signifies, like ישׁר, to be straight, even, fortunate, whence אשׁר = Arab. yusâr, happiness, and to step straight out, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.6">Pro 9:6</reference>, of which meanings אשּׁר is partly the intensive, as here, partly the causative, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.19">Pro 23:19</reference> (elsewhere causative of the meaning, to be happy, <reference osisRef="Gen.30.13">Gen 30:13</reference>). The meaning <hi type="italic">progredi</hi> is not mediated by a supplementary צעדיו; the derivative אשׁוּר (אשּׁוּר), a step, shows that it is derived immediately from the root-idea of a movement in a straight line. Still less justifiable is the rendering by Schultens, <hi type="italic">ne vestigia imprimas in via malorum</hi>; for the Arab. âththr is denom. of ithr, אתר, the primitive verb roots of which, athr, אתר = אשׁר, are lost.
entries.93a4210939540531ff00bb1b497dd139b7162b07: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.15">Pro 4:15</reference> <div eID="gen10675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10676" type="x-p"/> On פּרעהוּ, avoid it (the way), (<hi type="italic">opp</hi>. אחז, <reference osisRef="Job.17.9">Job 17:9</reference>; תּמך, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.5">Psa 17:5</reference>), see under Pro 1:25. שׂטה, elsewhere (as the Arab. shatt, to be without measure, insolent) used <hi type="italic">in malam partem</hi>, has here its fundamental meaning, to go aside. מעליו (expressed in French by <hi type="italic">de dessus</hi>, in Ital. by <hi type="italic">di sopra</hi>) denotes: so that thou comest not to stand on it. עבר means in both cases <hi type="italic">transire</hi>, but the second instance, “to go beyond (farther)” (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.22">2Sa 15:22</reference>, and under <reference osisRef="Hab.1.11">Hab 1:11</reference>), coincides with “to escape, <hi type="italic">evadere</hi>.”
entries.bce16ff785b25ec6b89ad4b5e3cfa1fe728c5170: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.16">Pro 4:16</reference> <div eID="gen10676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10677" type="x-p"/> In the reason here given the perf. may stand in the conditional clauses as well as in Virgil’s <hi type="italic">Et si non aliqua nocuisses, mortuus esses</hi>; but the fut., as in <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.11">Ecc 5:11</reference>, denotes that they (the רעים and the רשׁעים) cannot sleep, and are deprived of their sleep, unless they are continually doing evil and bringing others into misery; the interruption of this course of conduct, which has become to them like a second nature, would be as the interruption of their diet, which makes them ill. For the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> יכשׁולוּ, which here must have the meaning of the person sinning (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.4.19">Pro 4:19</reference>), and would be feeble if used of the confirmed transgressors, the Kerı̂ rightly substitutes the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> יכשׁילוּ, which occurs also <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.8">2Ch 25:8</reference>, there without an object, in the meaning to cause to fall, as the contrast of עזר (to help).
entries.340a7f6fa0e92a10889050cb32c9c221ff5dd993: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.17">Pro 4:17</reference> <div eID="gen10677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10678" type="x-p"/> The second כּי introduces the reason of their bodily welfare being conditioned by evil-doing. If the poet meant: they live on bread which consists in wickedness, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, on wickedness as their bread, then in the parallel sentence he should have used the word חמס; the genitives are meant of the means of acquisition: they live on unrighteous gain, on bread and wine which they procure by wickedness and by all manner of violence or injustice. On the etymon of חמס (Arab. ḥamas, <hi type="italic">durum, asperum, vehementem esse</hi>), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Schultens; the plur. חמסים belongs to a more recent epoch (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.49">2Sa 22:49</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.18.49">Psa 18:49</reference>). The change in the tense represents the idea that they having eaten such bread, set forth such wine, and therewith wash it down.
entries.0d946d7c6f7dcc2f8f6172d233bf17b296d78730: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.18-Prov.4.19">Pro 4:18-19</reference> <div eID="gen10678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10679" type="x-p"/> The two ways that lie for his choice before the youth, are distinguished from one another as light is from darkness: 18 And the path of the just is like the brightness of the morning light,      Which shines more and more till the perfect day. 19 The way of the wicked is deep darkness,      They know not at what they stumble. <div eID="gen10679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10680" type="x-p"/> The Hebr. style is wont to conceal in its <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> (ו) diverse kinds of logical relations, but the <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> of 18a may suitably stand before 19a, where the discontinuance of this contrast of the two ways is unsuitable. The displacing of a <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> from its right position is not indeed without example (see under <reference osisRef="Ps.16.3">Psa 16:3</reference>); but since <reference osisRef="Prov.4.19">Pro 4:19</reference> joins itself more easily than <reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Pro 4:18</reference> to <reference osisRef="Prov.4.17">Pro 4:17</reference> without missing a particle, thus it is more probable that the two verses are to be transposed, than that the ו of וארח (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.17">Pro 4:17</reference>) is to be prefixed to דּרך (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Pro 4:18</reference>). Sinning, says <reference osisRef="Prov.4.16">Pro 4:16</reference>, has become to the godless as a second nature, so that they cannot sleep without it; they must continually be sinning, adds <reference osisRef="Prov.4.17">Pro 4:17</reference>, for thus and not otherwise do they gain for themselves their daily bread. With reference to this fearful self-perversion to which wickedness has become a necessity and a condition of life, the poet further says that the way of the godless is כּאפלה,<note placement="foot">In good MSS and printed copies the כ has the <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi>, as Kimchi states the rule in <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 45a: כל כּאפלה פתח, כל כּאבנים פתח.</note> as deep darkness, as the entire absence of light: it cannot be otherwise than that they fall, but they do not at all know whereat they fall, for they do not at all know wickedness as such, and have no apprehension of the punishment which from an inward necessity it brings along with it; on the contrary, the path of the just is in constantly increasing light - the light of knowledge, and the light of true happiness which is given<note placement="foot">Hitzig inverts the order of <reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Pro 4:18</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.4.19">Pro 4:19</reference>, and connects the כּי of 16a immediately with <reference osisRef="Prov.4.19">Pro 4:19</reference> (for the way of the wicked...). He moreover regards <reference osisRef="Prov.4.16">Pro 4:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.17">Pro 4:17</reference> as an interpolation, and explains <reference osisRef="Prov.4.16">Pro 4:16</reference> as a gloss transforming the text of Pro 4:19. “That the wicked commit wickedness,” says Hitzig, “is indeed certain (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.14">1Sa 24:14</reference>), and the warning of <reference osisRef="Prov.4.15">Pro 4:15</reference> ought not to derive its motive from their energy in sinning.” But the warning against the way of the wicked is founded not on their energy in sinning, but on their bondage to sin: their sleep, their food and drink - their life both when they sleep and when they wake - is conditioned by sin and is penetrated by sin. This foundation of the warning furnishes what is needed, and is in nothing open to objection. And that in <reference osisRef="Prov.4.16">Pro 4:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.4.19">Pro 4:19</reference> לא ירעוּ and לא ידעוּ, יכשׁולוּ and יכּשׁלוּ, נגזלה and כּאפלה seem to be alike, does not prove that <reference osisRef="Prov.4.16">Pro 4:16</reference> originated as a parallel text from <reference osisRef="Prov.4.19">Pro 4:19</reference> - in the one verse as in the other the thoughts are original.</note> in and with knowledge. On בּמּה <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Isa.2.22">Isa 2:22</reference>; it is מכשׁול, σκάνδαλον, that is meant, stumbling against which (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.26.37">Lev 26:37</reference>) they stumble to their fall. נגהּ,<note placement="foot">Böttcher, under <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2Sa 23:4</reference>, explains נגהּ of the brightness striking against, conquering (cf. נגח, נגף) the clouds; but <hi type="italic">ferire</hi> or <hi type="italic">percutere</hi> lies nearer (cf. נגע, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.10">Eze 17:10</reference>, נכה, <reference osisRef="Ps.121.6">Psa 121:6</reference>, and the Arab. darb, used of strong sensible impressions), as Silius, iv. 329, says of the light: <hi type="italic">percussit lumine campos</hi>.</note> used elsewhere than in the Bible, means the morning star (Venus), (Sirach 50:4, Syr.); when used in the Bible it means the early dawn, the light of the rising sun, the morning light, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2Sa 23:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.1">Isa 62:1</reference>, which announces itself in the morning twilight, Dan 6:20. The light of this morning sunshine is הולך ואור, going and shining, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, becoming ever brighter. In the connection of הולך ואור it might be a question whether אור is regarded as gerundive (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.3">Gen 8:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.8.5">Gen 8:5</reference>), or as participle (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.5">2Sa 16:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.41.6">Jer 41:6</reference>), or as a participial adjective (<reference osisRef="Gen.26.13">Gen 26:13</reference>; Jdg 4:24); in the connection of הלוך ואור, on the contrary, it is unquestionably the gerundive: the partic. denoting the progress joins itself either with the partic., <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.11">Jon 1:11</reference>, or with the participial adjective, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.1">2Sa 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.12">2Ch 17:12</reference>, or with another adjective formation, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.12">2Sa 15:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.9.4">Est 9:4</reference> (where וגדול after וגדל of other places appears to be intended as an adjective, not after <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.10">2Sa 5:10</reference> as gerundive). Thus ואור, as also וטוב, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.26">1Sa 2:26</reference>, will be participial after the form בּושׁ, being ashamed (Ges. §72, 1); cf. בּוס, Zec 10:5, קום, 2Ki 16:7. “נכון היּום quite corresponds to the Greek τὸ σταθηρὸν τῆς ἡμέρας, ἡ σταθηρὰ μεσημβρία (as one also says τὸ σταθηρὸν τῆς νυκτός), and to the Arabic qâ'mt ‛l-nhâr and qâ'mt ‛l-dhyrt. The figure is probably derived from the balance (cf. Lucan’s <hi type="italic">Pharsalia</hi>, lib. 9: <hi type="italic">quam cardine summo Stat librata dies</hi>): before and after midday the tongue on the balance of the day bends to the left and to the right, but at the point of midday it stands directly in the midst” (Fleischer). It is the midday time that is meant, when the clearness of the day has reached its fullest intensity - the point between increasing and decreasing, when, as we are wont to say, the sun stands in the zenith (= Arab. samt, the point of support, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the vertex). Besides <reference osisRef="Mark.4.28">Mar 4:28</reference>, there is no biblical passage which presents like these two a figure of gradual development. The progress of blissful knowledge is compared to that of the clearness of the day till it reaches its midday height, having reached to which it becomes a knowing of all in God, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.5">Pro 28:5</reference>; 1Jo 2:20.
entries.66aa86678d885127aa1cc988caef3ef5ad8c26f1: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.20-Prov.4.22">Pro 4:20-22</reference> <div eID="gen10680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10681" type="x-p"/> The paternal admonition now takes a new departure: 20 My son, attend unto my words,      Incline thine ear to my sayings. 21 Let them not depart from thine eyes;      Keep them in the midst of thine heart. 22 For they are life to all who get possession of them,      And health to their whole body. <div eID="gen10681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10682" type="x-p"/> Regarding the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הלּין (for הלין), <reference osisRef="Prov.4.21">Pro 4:21</reference>, formed after the Chaldee manner like הלּין, הנּיח, הסּיג, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Gesenius, §72, 9; - Ewald, §114, c, gives to it the meaning of “to mock,” for he interchanges it with הלין, instead of the meaning to take away, <hi type="italic">efficere ut recedat</hi> (cf. under <reference osisRef="Prov.2.15">Pro 2:15</reference>). This supposed causative meaning it has also here: may they = may one (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Prov.2.22">Pro 2:22</reference>) not remove them from thine eyes; the object is (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.20">Pro 4:20</reference>) the words of the paternal admonition. Hitzig, indeed, observes that “the accusative is not supplied;” but with greater right it is to be remarked that ילּיזוּ (fut. <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. of לוּז) and ילוּזוּ (fut. <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> of <hi type="italic">id</hi>.) are not one and the same, and the less so as הלּיז occurs, but the masoretical and grammatical authorities (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Kimchi) demand ילּיזוּ. The plur. למצאיהם is continued, 22b, in the sing., for that which is said refers to each one of the many (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.18">Pro 3:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.28">Pro 3:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.35">Pro 3:35</reference>). מצא is fundamentally an active conception, like our “<hi type="italic">finden</hi>,” to find; it means to attain, to produce, to procure, etc. מרפּא means, according as the מ is understood of the “that = <hi type="italic">ut</hi>” of the action or of the “what” of its performance, either health or the means of health; here, like רפאוּת, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.8">Pro 3:8</reference>, not with the underlying conception of sickness, but of the fluctuations connected with the bodily life of man, which make needful not only a continual strengthening of it, but also its being again and again restored. Nothing preserves soul and body in a healthier state than when we always keep before our eyes and carry in our hearts the good doctrines; they give to us true guidance on the way of life: “Godliness has the promise of this life, and of that which is to come.” 1Ti 4:8.
entries.db996c36409ed21ea7a49298bbd90ec044839afa: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.23-Prov.4.27">Pro 4:23-27</reference> <div eID="gen10682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10683" type="x-p"/> After this general preface the exhortation now becomes special: 23 Above all other things that are to be guarded, keep thy heart,      For out from it life has its issues. 24 Put away from thee perverseness of mouth,      And waywardness of lips put far from thee. 25 Thine eyes should look straight forward,      And thine eyelids look straight to the end before thee. 26 Make even the path of thy feet,      And let all thy ways be correct. 27 Turn not aside to the right and to the left;      Remove thy foot from evil. <div eID="gen10683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10684" type="x-p"/> Although משׁמר in itself and in this connection may mean the object to be watchfully avoided (<hi type="italic">cavendi</hi>) (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Prov.2.20">Pro 2:20</reference>): thus the usage of the language lying before us applies it, yet only as denoting the place of watching or the object <hi type="italic">observandi</hi>; so that it is not to be thus explained, with Raschi and others: before all from which one has to protect himself (<hi type="italic">ab omni re cavenda</hi>), guard thine heart; but: before all that one has to guard (<hi type="italic">prae omni re custodienda</hi>), guard it as the most precious of possessions committed to thy trust. The heart, which according to its etymon denotes that which is substantial (<hi type="italic">Kernhafte</hi>) in man (cf. Arab. lubb, the kernel of the nut or almond), comes here into view not as the physical, but as the intellectual, and specially the ethical <hi type="italic">centrum</hi>.

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. IV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1. HEar, ye children, the instruction of a father <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Of me your Teacher, who have paternal authority over you and affection to you.</ns0:note>, and attend to know understanding.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2. See on Chap. 3. 1.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3. For I was <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">

                     <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>onely,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>the onely Son:</ns0:hi> Or rather, because <ns0:hi>Bathsheba</ns0:hi> seems to have had other Sons, 1 <ns0:hi>Chro.</ns0:hi> 5. 1. <ns0:hi>as an onely Son,</ns0:hi> as dearly beloved as an onely Son: in which sense this Title is given to <ns0:hi>Isaac, Gen.</ns0:hi> 22. 2. 12, 16. though he had another Son, and to others. And all these circumstances are men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioned to shew the necessity and great benefit of wholesome instru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ction, which his Royal Parents would not neglect, no not in his tender years, and thereby to prepare and excite them by his ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ample to receive instruction.</ns0:note> in the sight of my mother.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Chr. 28. 9.</ns0:note> He taught me also, and said unto me <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The following Verses, at least as far as the Tenth Verse, are propounded as the words of <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> that the Name of so great a King and Holy a Prophet might add the more Authority and Efficacy to his Counsels.</ns0:note>, Let thine heart retain my words, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 7. 2.</ns0:note> keep my commandments and live <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Thou shalt live. It is a promise in the form of a command, as Chap. 3. 25.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5. Get wisdom, get understanding: forget <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> not, neither decline from the words of my mouth <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">From the belief and practice of my Word.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6. Forsake her not, and she shall preserve thee: love her <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">He intimates, that it is not enough to do what is good, which may somtimes proceed from worldly or sinful Motives, but that we must have a sincere and fervent love to it.</ns0:note>, and she shall keep thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7. Wisdom <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the principal thing <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">The most excellent of all possessions.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>therefore</ns0:hi> get wisdom: and with all <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Even with the price of all, though it cost thee the loss of all which thou hast. Or, <ns0:hi>in or among all.</ns0:hi> Whilst you labour for other things, do not neglect this.</ns0:note> thy <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>substance</ns0:hi> Ch. 23. 23.</ns0:note> getting get understand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8.                   <ns0:p n="9">9. She shall give to thine head <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 1. 9.</ns0:note> an ornament of grace <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> An acceptable or beautiful ornament, such as they used to put upon their heads.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> she shall compass thee with a Crown of Glory.</ns0:note> a crown of glory shall she deliver to thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10. Hear, O my son, and receive my sayings: and the years of thy life shall be many.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11. I have taught thee in the way of wisdom <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Either, 1. which precureth Wisdom. Or 2. which Wisdom directeth thee to walk in.</ns0:note>: I have led thee in right paths.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12. When thou goest, thy steps shall not be strait<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Thou shalt manage thine affairs with great facility and safe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty and success. Ch. 3. 23.</ns0:note> and when thou runnest, thou shalt not stum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Not mis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />carry.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 3. 18.</ns0:note> Take fast hold of instruction, let <ns0:hi>her</ns0:hi> not go; keep her, for she <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thy life <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The conducter, and preserver, and comfort of thy life.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 1. 1. Ch. 1. 10. 15.</ns0:note> Enter not into the path of the wicked <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Avoid their courses and company.</ns0:note>, and go not * in the way of evil <ns0:hi>men.</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>x</ns0:hi> Do not proceed further. If thou hast unadvisedly entred into it, do not persist in it, but get thee speedily out of it.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15. Avoid it, pass not by it <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Keep at a great distance from it. Compare <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 22. 23<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 5. 8.</ns0:note>, turn from it <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Shun all occasions of sin.</ns0:note>, and pass away.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 For they sleep not <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">They cannot compose themselves to sleep with quietness and satisaction to their own minds</ns0:note> except they have done mischief: and their sleep is taken away unless they cause some to fall <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Into their own Snares, either into sin, or into mischief.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:520" />17. For they eat the bread of wickedness <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The sense is either, 1. Wickedness is as necessary and as plea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sant to them as their Bread. Which suits well with the former Verse. Or, 2. They live wholly upon what they get by wicked courses. Which gives the reason of what he last said, why they could not sleep without prey.</ns0:note>, and drink the wine of violence <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Gotten by violence. See on the former Clause.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18. But the path of the just <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> as the shining light <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The common course of their lives or actions is pure and spotless, clear and certain, safe and comfortable, as light is.</ns0:note>, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Just men do daily more and more grow in knowledge, and grace, and consolation, until all be perfected and swallowed up in glory.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19.                   <ns0:p n="20">20. My Son, attend to my words: incline thine ear unto my sayings.</ns0:p>
